assessment.nobel_worthiness: Opening a new window on the universe: IceCube's detection of a diffuse flux of high-energy astrophysical neutrinos, and the association with the blazar TXS 0506+056 and the Galactic plane, are discoveries made from clues in nature, with clear existential and cosmological interest and a decades-long instrumental effort behind them.
assessment.attribution: Halzen was the scientific driver of IceCube and the AMANDA precursor and Spiering was a leader of the pioneering Baikal and AMANDA work and the collaboration's early development. Both fit a prize built around the instrument, but a large collaboration and other pioneers (not on the list) make the allocation delicate.
assessment.maturity: Diffuse flux confirmed by several analyses and by independent detectors at lower significance; source identification is still partial. Recognition is arguably timely for the detection and the technique, less so for the source astrophysics.
uncertainties: Only a few sources are firmly identified, so the astrophysics of the neutrino flux is still open.
Credit for pioneering neutrino telescopes (DUMAND, Baikal) extends beyond the two names supplied; I have not independently verified the detailed history.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The experimental discovery of the Higgs boson closed the Standard Model and confirmed the 2013 theoretical prize with a measurement in nature. It is of the first rank in importance, clarity and lasting impact, and two independent detectors confirmed it.
assessment.attribution: Della Negra (CMS) and Jenni (ATLAS) were founding spokespeople and conceivers of the detectors, and Gianotti led ATLAS at the time of the announcement. Tejinder Virdee is an equally strong CMS founder candidate, so any three-person split between the two experiments is uneasy and a collaboration-level award is a known problem.
assessment.maturity: Fully mature: measured couplings and properties confirmed by two experiments over more than a decade. Timing is fine and only constrained by the three-person limit.
uncertainties: Whether the committee can fairly honour two experiments with three names; the choice among CMS and ATLAS founders is contestable.
The LHC machine builders might claim a part of the credit.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The first horizon-scale images of M87* and Sgr A* are direct observational clues about black holes, which are close to my own research interests, and test strong-field gravity. The impact on astrophysics and gravity is large, and the images are easily communicated.
assessment.attribution: Falcke proposed the shadow-imaging idea, Doeleman built the mm-VLBI capability and led the EHT, and Moran pioneered the interferometry and the SMA/VLBI technology. Credit is spread over a large collaboration, so the three-name configuration is plausible but not unique.
assessment.maturity: Two sources imaged and multi-epoch consistency checks done, but the interpretation of the ring and the astrophysical modelling are still developing. Timely, perhaps slightly early for a prize.
uncertainties: Large collaboration; the proper choice of individuals is disputed.
Whether the prize would rest on a technical achievement or a physics discovery given the models needed for interpretation.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum key distribution is the founding result of quantum cryptography and bridges foundations (Bell-type arguments) and technology. Importance is high and the idea was original and clear, and it has spawned a whole field.
assessment.attribution: BB84 by Bennett and Brassard and the entanglement-based protocol by Ekert form a natural trio. The listing has two spellings for Ekert, which I treat as one person and use the plain 'Artur Ekert' string.
assessment.maturity: Experimentally demonstrated over fibre and satellite links, with commercial systems, but practical security remains debated and the recent 2022 prize already covered Bell-test experiments, so recognition is somewhat overlapping.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2022 prize on entanglement and quantum information.
Real-world security loopholes and its mostly engineering application make it a theory-heavy choice, and Wiesner's earlier ideas also play a role.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks at the 10^-18 level are a leap in precision measurement and enable tests of fundamental constants, relativistic redshift at millimetre scales and potential dark-matter searches. Clear and lasting.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice concept and Ye achieved record precision. A two-person prize is clean, though Hall and Hänsch (2005) and the ion-clock community already received related recognition.
assessment.maturity: Mature and independently reproduced in many laboratories, with an international redefinition of the second under discussion. Timely.
uncertainties: Overlap with prior frequency-comb and ion-clock prizes.
Others (e.g. lattice proposals from different groups) may claim some credit; I have not verified the priority details.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Kilonovae link the neutron-star merger GW170817 to the r-process origin of heavy elements such as gold, which is a clear answer to a long-standing question about where the elements come from, with an existential dimension.
assessment.attribution: Lattimer (early prediction of decompression ejecta), Metzger (kilonova modelling) and Tanvir (observational kilonova identification) would give a theory and observation mix. Kasen's role is also decisive, so the selection is contestable.
assessment.maturity: Strong support from AT2017gfo, but only one clean event with multi-messenger data and the quantitative r-process yields remain uncertain, so it may be premature as a separate prize while GW/LIGO was recognised in 2017.
uncertainties: Single well-observed event; the contribution of mergers to the cosmic r-process abundances is uncertain.
Overlap with the 2017 gravitational-wave prize and a disputed split among the theorists.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Baryon acoustic oscillations are a robust standard ruler that fixes the expansion history and provides key constraints on dark energy, a topic of great concern to me. The result rests on real clues from galaxy surveys.
assessment.attribution: Eisenstein (SDSS detection), Cole and Percival (2dFGRS analysis) were the first detections in 2005, while Peacock and others contributed too. The theoretical idea itself goes back to Peebles, Yu and Sunyaev and Zeldovich, so credit is muddled.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed by many surveys (SDSS, BOSS, DESI), and the 2011 prize covered accelerated expansion. Recent DESI hints of evolving dark energy could change the interpretation, so the maturity is good for the standard ruler but not for what it implies.
uncertainties: Priority of the theoretical idea belongs to people outside the credited set.
Evolving dark energy hints from recent BAO data are still unsettled.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Transmission spectroscopy of exoplanet atmospheres, with detection of sodium and water, is a real step toward understanding other worlds and the question of life, though the 2019 prize already recognised exoplanet discovery.
assessment.attribution: Seager (theory of atmospheric signatures) and Charbonneau (first atmosphere detection, HD 209458b) are the clear pair, and Tinetti is a less clear third. The list has a distinct HD 209458b-related entry, which suggests possible overlap.
assessment.maturity: The field is rapidly maturing with JWST, with many independent confirmations, though some early detections were revised. It may be a little early as the strongest results come from the current decade.
uncertainties: Overlap with candidate B009 and with the 2019 exoplanet prize.
Some early atmospheric detections have been questioned; I have not verified the history.
